report:
I have solid, converging evidence. Let me finalize.

## Conclusion: Largely Yes — with caveats

The evidence supports the claim, but the effect is modest and depends heavily on the population and product used.

**Strongest evidence (Cochrane, 2023 update):** The most authoritative source, the Cochrane systematic review of 50 RCTs (~8,857 participants), found cranberry products (juice or capsules) reduce the risk of repeat, symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs by about 26% compared with placebo/no treatment, specifically in women with recurrent UTIs, children, and people susceptible to UTIs following interventions like radiotherapy ([cochrane.org](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001321_cranberries-preventing-urinary-tract-infections), [cochranelibrary.com](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD001321.pub6/full)). Notably, this update reversed the previous (2012) Cochrane conclusion that cranberry had no benefit, largely because newer trials used higher, more consistent doses of active proanthocyanidins (PACs).

**Supporting meta-analysis:** A separate 2017 meta-analysis (funded by a cranberry industry sponsor, a limitation to note) reached a similar conclusion for otherwise healthy women with recurrent UTI ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29046404](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29046404/)).

**Dose matters:** A randomized double-blind trial comparing high-dose (72mg) versus low-dose (36mg) standardized cranberry PAC extract found the higher dose was more effective at preventing recurrence, suggesting standardized PAC content — not just "cranberry juice" generically — drives efficacy ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12894-021-00811-w)).

**Important caveat — population-specific:** Benefit is NOT universal. A rigorous RCT in older women in nursing homes found cranberry capsules showed no significant benefit for bacteriuria/pyuria reduction ([sciencedaily.com](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/10/161027122301.htm)), indicating efficacy is strongest in younger, otherwise healthy women with recurrent cystitis rather than frail elderly populations.

**Bottom line:** For generally healthy women prone to recurrent cystitis, regular cranberry intake (particularly standardized PAC extracts) modestly reduces UTI recurrence risk. It's not a cure-all, but current best evidence supports it as a reasonable preventive strategy.
